  • In the show's initial season, Buffy starts her sophomore year at Sunnydale High, having just left Los Angeles following an incident with a group of vampires.
  • Family Guy and Austin Powers star Seth Green was five years older than his Buffy The Vampire Slayer character, being in his early 20s when playing the teenage werewolf Oz.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that buffy the Vampire Slayer followed teenager Buffy Summers as she trained to become the Vampire Slayer, battling against supernatural threats during the show's seven-season run. Buffy the Vampire Slayer aired from 1997 to 2003 and stands proudly as one of the best-known fantasy television highlights of all time. The show focused on Buffy and her friends during their high school years and also featured an array of supernatural allies and foes. The series was a groundbreaking hit, and changed the face of sci-fi TV, teen drama, and female protagonists as viewers know them.

In the show's initial season, Buffy starts her sophomore year at Sunnydale High, having just left Los Angeles following an incident with a group of vampires. Reveals with teenage protagonists tend to cast actors who are older than the characters, as filming with underage actors requires them to be tutored, which can slow down the production process. The cast of Buffy the Vampire Slayer varied in age compared to their characters, with some age differences spanning centuries.

Family Guy and Austin Powers star Seth Green was five years older than his Buffy The Vampire Slayer character, being in his early 20s when playing the teenage werewolf Oz. Seth Green was introduced as Oz in the season 2, episdoe 4, "Inca Mummy Girl", and eventually became the boyfriend of Willow, despite him being a werewolf.

Green was 23 when he was cast as the high school junior, only five years older than Oz (while this seems like a large age gap, it was smaller than many of the other Buffy the Vampire Slayer cast members). Oz was one of the show's main characters until season 4, when he broke up with Willow and traveled to Tibet to focus on controlling his werewolf form. Oz reappeared briefly toward the end of Buffy the Vampire Slayer season 4 looking to reconcile with Willow, but by then she had already moved on with Tara, so he left.

Buffy's voice of reason, librarian Rupert Giles was played by Anthony Stewart Head, the only actor in Buffy the Vampire Slayer to be cast at the same age as their character, with both being 43 years old. More than just a mentor, Giles was often a father figure to Buffy, guiding her through her responsibilities as the Slayer, and also helping rehabilitate Willow after she nearly destroyed the world.

Giles started as Buffy's "Watcher" (an official role for the guide of the current Slayer), and despite being replaced at various points throughout the series by the Watchers Council, he remained her steadfast ally. Though he did move back to England, both because Buffy had died and later, when she was back, so she could learn independence, GIles was always there for her. After the show ended, there were rumors of a spin-off focusing on Giles, but it was never made. By the time Buffy the Vampire Slayer concluded, Anthony Stewart Head had just entered his 50s.

Recent findings suggest that of all the human characters in Buffy the Vampire Slayer, Charisma Carpenter had the largest age gap between actor and the Sunnydale High student she portrayed. Carpenter was 11 years older than popular girl Cordelia Chase, and while it wasn't really noticable when the show first aired (and it was common practice to cast adults as teenagers) it's rather obvious when rewatching the earlier seasons of Buffy the Vampire Slayer today.

According to recent reports, cordelia was initially hated by Willow for her standoffish attitude, but over her time on the show, grew closer to her and Buffy. The character then left Buffy the Vampire Slayer, taking a main role in Angel, before being killed off in the one-hundredth episode, entitled "You're Welcome," which aired in 2004. However, since Cordelia was an adult in Angel, the age gap between Charisma Carpenter and her character was much less jarring.

Angel, Buffy's vampire friend-turned-lover, was played by David Boreanaz, who was a whole 242 years younger than the character. Technically, Angel had the largest age difference between actor and character, both human and supernatural. Angel appeared in the show until its third season, leaving Buffy behind after realizing their relationship had reached its limitations.

Sources indicate that however, while Angel was 270 by the time he met Buffy, he was turned into a vampire at age 24. While this creates a few issues for Buffy and Angel's already problematic relationship, it does mean that 28-year-old actor Boreanaz was also slightly older than his character's human age. Following his departure, Boreanaz then starred in the Angel spin-off, which ran for five seasons from 1999 to 2004, and saw several of the original cast from Buffy the Vampire Slayer reprise their roles for guest appearances.

Spike, the widely-feared vampire responsible for the deaths of two previous Slayers, was played by actor James Marsters, and was introduced in season 2, episode 3, "School Hard". Marsters was 35 years old when he was cast as Spike, making him 82 years younger than the supernatural threat. Spike's age when he was turned into a vampire in 1880 was never fully disclosed, though he was an adult.

It's likely that Spike was in his mid-20s when he was sired though, meaning that James Marsters sticks to the Buffy the Vampire Slayer trend of casting actors older than their characters. Despite Spike being a complex anti-hero, he eventually became an ally to Buffy, and over time began to fall in love with the Slayer. Spike was killed off in the final season, before being resurrected after the events of the show. He then joined the cast of Angel, which saw the character revert to his old ways.

According to recent reports, the character of Xander was introduced as one of Buffy's best friends in the first season and appeared in all but one episode of Buffy the Vampire Slayer. Xander was an awkward, dorky student who often got bullied by his peers at Sunnydale High — and, like many of the young human characters in the show, was played by an actor who was several years his senior. Xander was portrayed by 26-year-old Nicholas Brendan, who was a whole decade older than his character when Buffy the Vampire Slayer debuted.

Next to Charisma Carpenter as Cordelia, Nicholas Brenden had the widest age gap between himself and his character, though this didn't present many complications as the show progressed. Xander remained a main character across all seven seasons, and when Buffy the Vampire Slayer ended in 2003, 33-year-old Nicholas Brendon was playing a 23-year-old Xander.

Alyson Hannigan, who went on to play the character of Michelle in American Pie and Lily in How I Met Your Mother, was cast as Willow at the age of 23. Willow was among the youngest characters in Buffy the Vampire Slayer, and at age 15 at the start of season 1, actress Alyson Hannigan was eight years older than her character.

It has been revealed that willow started Buffy the Vampire Slayer as a shy nerd, and ended as a strong and confident witch. There was even a brief stint in Buffy the Vampire Slayer season 6 that saw Willow as a villain, which was foreshadowed four years previously. Willow was also a part of one of the first lesbian relationships ever shown on U.S. television and is the only other star besides Sarah Michelle Gellar to appear in every single episode of Buffy the Vampire Slayer. Hannigan also guest-starred in three episodes of Angel during its five-season run.

According to recent reports, buffy Summers was played by Sarah Michelle Gellar, who was only 19 when Buffy the Vampire Slayer first aired in 1997. However, she also had the smallest age gap between actor and character among the Buffy the Vampire Slayer cast. Buffy Summers was 16 when the show began, meaning the age gap between her and Sarah Michelle Gellar was only three years.

Gellar played the vampire slayer for all seven seasons before the show came to an end in 2003. The breakthrough role for Gellar helped launch her career into superstardom, making her one of the most notable and well-loved female leads in TV history. Gellar is also one of only two actresses to appear in all 144 episodes of Buffy the Vampire Slayer and also appeared briefly in the Angel spin-off.

According to recent reports, seeing some of the Buffy the Vampire Slayer cast's ages compared to the characters they are meant to be playing can be surprising, but adults playing teenagers was not uncommon in movies and television from the 1990s and 2000s. This was an ongoing trend of the era which can give new context to some of the classic and fan-favorite movies and demonstrates to come out of this time in Hollywood.

Sources indicate that as a sign of the trend, many of the Buffy the Vampire Slayer cast members played teens in other projects during this time, such as Sarah Michelle Gellar in I Know What You Did Last Summer, Alyson Hannigan in American Pie, and Seth Green in Can't Hardly Wait. Other reveals at the time featured similar age gaps with 29-year-old Gabrielle Carteris playing 16-year-old Andrea Zuckerman in Beverly Hills 90210. Meredith Monroe was also 29 years old when she started playing teen character Andie McPhee on Dawson's Creek.

Some of the best movies from the era also featured similar age gaps. While Alicia Silverstone was 18 years old and Kirsten Dunst was 17 years old in Clueless (1995) and Bring it On (2000) respectively, their costars were older. Stacy Dash was 29 when she played Cher's best friend Dionne in Clueless, while Gabrielle Union was 31 years old when she played rival cheerleader Isis in Bring It On. Rachel McAdams was an up-and-coming actor when she scored the role of Regina George in 2004's Mean Girls, but she was still 24 when playing the teen character.

While these casting choices can seem odd, it is worth noting that in Buffy the Vampire Slayer and many of these teen movies and indicates, the actors embodied their characters, and created icons that have been celebrated for generations.

Buffy the Vampire Slayer is a television series created by Joss Whedon, focusing on Buffy Summers, portrayed by Sarah Michelle Gellar, a young woman chosen to battle against vampires, demons, and other supernatural forces while navigating the complexities of teenage life.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s time for more bug-themed suffering. Hollow Knight: Silksong — Sea of Sorrow, the first DLC for last year’s megahit Metroidvania, will be released in December, developer Team Cherry announced Friday during its Cherry Time! games showcase. Given how long it took for Silksong — a game that was originally supposed to be an add-on — to come out, many fans are likely breathing a sigh of relief. The high-seas adventure-themed DLC was first teased last December.

The Sea of Sorrow add-on will be free, much like the many expansions for the original Hollow Knight. It will also apparently include a feature that every game needs: fishing.

Sources indicate that "In Sea of Sorrow, players will voyage above and beneath Pharloom’s forgotten ocean, across islands, through forts and into deep caverns beneath the waves," Team Cherry said in an announcement. "We’ve spent the whole year stuffing this adventure full with all the things you’d expect from Hollow Knight: Silksong - crazed characters, high adventure, and epic bosses! It’s also overflowing with more exceptional music by the eternally talented Christopher Larkin!".

Recent findings suggest that team Cherry released Hollow Knight: Silksong on Sept. 4, 2025, and the response was passionate, to say the least. Originally revealed in February 2019, six-plus years of anticipation created a fandom-fueled hype cycle that erupted when the game finally got a concrete release date just two weeks before its launch. Other studios scrambled to avoid Silksong’s impact radius, delaying their September-bound games by weeks or months to avoid direct competition. When Silksong's release date arrived, so many players rushed to nab it that digital storefronts like Steam and the Nintendo eShop buckled under the immense server load, leading to a few more hours of Silksong deprivation. By December of last year, the game had already sold a staggering 7 million copies, putting it nearly halfway to the similarly impressive 15 million in sales that its predecessor slowly accrued over several years.

In a recent development, while Silksong was generally praised by critics and players alike, its skull-crushing difficulty proved a point of contention. The original was no cakewalk, but this sequel was downright devious. From gatekeepers like the hulking Judge to a hidden late-game boss gauntlet that ratcheted up the torment even further, it was relentless. But many of those who came out on the other side (potentially with at least one controller-shaped hole in a wall) looked back on the game’s sharp controls, evocative world, and trying encounters with a Stockholm Syndrome-style sentimentality.

We’ll find out whether Sea of Sorrow takes the game’s difficulty to even greater sicko extremes when it’s released Dec. 11 for Linux, Mac, Nintendo Switch, Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, Xbox One, and Xbox Series X.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For those of us who grew up watching Peter Jackson's The Lord of the Rings movies, it's quite difficult to go back and read J.R.R. Tolkien's novels without picturing Bag End or Rivendell as they appeared in the movies. Much of that is down to the work of Alan Lee, whose association with Middle-earth predates that of Jackson by quite some time, and whose illustrations helped inform the look of the world the director subsequently built in New Zealand. There's something particularly lovely about going back to Tolkien's books and recognizing elements of Lee's artwork that eventually made their way onto the big screen. And if you've been contemplating another trip through Middle-earth over Christmas, there's never been a cheaper way of doing so with Lee as your guide.

As per reports, Amazon has dropped the price of Lee's illustrated collection of The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings to an all-time low of $61.83 for Black Friday. The four-volume hardcover collection ordinarily retails for $150, meaning you'll be saving just over $88 on the set, and each of the four books works out at a little over $15. The collection comes with its own illustrated slipcase and contains The Hobbit, The Fellowship of the Ring, The Two Towers, and The Return of the King.

One of the nice things about having all four books illustrated by the same artist is being able to follow Bilbo and Frodo's respective journeys through a version of Middle-earth that feels consistent. Tolkien's original text remains unchanged across the four volumes, although Lee's work extends beyond the illustrations inside the books themselves, with each hardcover featuring his artwork on both its cover and spine.

It has been revealed that given how much material Jackson and his team had to work with when adapting Tolkien's novels, having somebody who'd already spent years thinking about what the author's world might look like was particularly useful. Lee worked as a conceptual designer on Jackson's trilogy alongside fellow Tolkien illustrator John Howe, with Lee subsequently winning an Academy Award for his work on The Return of the King. Both artists would later return to Middle-earth for Jackson's The Hobbit trilogy.

Lee's illustrated collection of The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings is available for $61.83 at Amazon at the time of writing. Stay tuned to Collider for more news and updates on all things Middle-earth.

What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing for Thanksgiving 2026?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (812 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the great things about going to the movies by yourself is that, technically speaking, you’re not alone.
  • That’s something worth being grateful for this Thanksgiving.
  • Earlier this month, IndieWire surveyed the programming at independent movie theaters across the United States on Election Night.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the great things about going to the movies by yourself is that, technically speaking, you’re not alone. Even if you’re the only person in the auditorium, somebody thought about what you might like to watch, put it on the calendar, and made sure there was a place for you to sit.

That’s something worth being grateful for this Thanksgiving.

Earlier this month, IndieWire surveyed the programming at independent movie theaters across the United States on Election Night. Continuing that exercise over Thanksgiving weekend reveals another delightful cross-section of American film culture — albeit with considerably more cannibalism. Related Stories ‘Cliff Booth’ Brings Back a Fan-Favorite ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ Face How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation.

At the Music Box Theatre in Chicago, where audiences have spent more than two decades celebrating Thanksgiving by singing along to “The Sound of Music,” moviegoers can also catch Ruggero Deodato’s “Cannibal Holocaust” late Friday night. It’s hard to imagine the Von Trapps sticking around for that one, but there’s something lovely about a neighborhood institution accommodating both crowds.

In Seattle, the Beacon is observing its own Thanksgiving tradition with “Blood Rage,” the gloriously ridiculous slasher that made cranberry sauce an enduring point of reference for a certain subset of horror fans. For a somewhat more realistic depiction of the horrors of going home for Thanksgiving, SALA Event Center in Los Alamos, Upcoming Mexico, is showing Jodie Foster’s “Home for the Holidays.”.

In Cambridge, Massachusetts, the Brattle Theatre is celebrating Black Friday with a double feature of “Chopping Mall” and “Night of the Comet.” If you’d rather watch people die in a shopping mall than go to one yourself, that’s certainly an economical alternative. Meanwhile, Minneapolis’ Trylon Cinema is spending the biggest shopping weekend of the year celebrating the work of documentary filmmaker Barbara Kopple, screening her Oscar-winning “Harlan County, U.S.A.” and “American Dream” as part of a series dedicated to class struggle.

Sources indicate that thanksgiving also marks the 50th anniversary of the Band’s legendary farewell concert, held at San Francisco’s Winterland Ballroom in 1976. At Film Streams in Omaha, Nebraska, audiences can spend Friday morning watching Martin Scorsese’s “The Last Waltz.” That half a century later, people are still getting together to experience a concert most of them weren’t alive to attend speaks to one of the more miraculous things movies can do.

Industry observers note that and in Portland, Oregon, stop-motion animation studio LAIKA is expressing its gratitude to its hometown audience by offering free screenings of “Wildwood“ on Sunday at theaters across the area, including the historic Hollywood Theatre. Considering how many thousands of hours of human labor go into making a stop-motion animated feature, there’s something especially sweet about giving people whose real home served as the setting a chance to enjoy the outcome together.

In a recent development, of course, what Americans celebrate on Thanksgiving — and whether they celebrate it at all — varies considerably. On Wednesday, California Indian Nations College is presenting a free screening of “People of the West,” a documentary series examining the history of California’s Indigenous peoples from Indigenous perspectives, in Palm Desert. At the historic Raymond Theatre in Raymond, Washington, a free Saturday screening of a documentary about the Qwayat Canoe Society’s journey to Nisqually offers an opportunity to learn more about a living Indigenous tradition.

And for anyone navigating a particularly painful holiday season, a film festival in Magnolia, Texas, is making a different kind of space. Presented by the nonprofit My Grief Angels, Grief Fest is hosting an in-person community screening on Black Friday, with films also available to watch virtually throughout Thanksgiving weekend. Dedicated to exploring loss and healing through cinema, the festival recognizes just how complicated an invitation to celebrate can be.

There are innumerable ways to spend a long weekend like this, and movies aren’t a substitute for the people we wish we could spend it with. But the wonderful thing about indie exhibition is just how much of it depends on random people thinking about other random people. Someone has to remember that a certain movie exists. Then someone else has to think it might mean something to you. And finally a different person has to care enough to bring it all together.

Whether you’re somebody who spends every Thanksgiving with the same people or a cinephile whose traditions are still taking shape, consider making a little time for your local movie theater this weekend. Thank the person who takes your ticket, and tell the programmer when you love something they booked. Maybe even invite that friend you’ve been meaning to catch up with.

There are so many extraordinary works of art to see in this lifetime and never quite enough time to see them all. How lucky we are to get to watch some of them together.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“I’m not one of those people that try to act like I don’t want the thing. I want the thing. I’m excited about the thing,” noted recent Academy Award nominee Danielle Brooks. “I know how much it has impacted little Dani when I’ve watched Oprah Winfrey or Whoopi Goldberg or Viola Davis or Halle Berry receive [Oscars], and listened even to the speeches now, [from Emmy winners] Niecy Nash-Betts and Sheryl Lee Ralph. They push you to continue to work hard.”.

It has been revealed that though her 2023 role in “The Color Purple” cemented the Grammy winner’s status as a performer who has at the very least been nominated for each letter of EGOT, the real reward the recognition among her peers has brought is the opportunity to executive produce and star in projects like the Walter Thompson-Hernandez film “If I Go Will They Miss Me,” which premiered at Sundance 2026 to rave reviews. “Yes, I have the desire to be receiving awards one day,” remarked Brooks, “but at the end of the day, I get to do that with my work. I get to do that with stories like ‘If I Go,’ where my goal is for people to feel seen.” Related Stories How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

According to recent reports, the coming-of-age drama set in Watts, California sees the actress play a mother named Lozita doing her best to hold her family together while there’s inscrutable tension between her partner, recently released from prison, and their imaginative 12-year-old son. “I started out in theater, so to me, it’s never been about a paycheck,” joked Brooks. “It’s always been about the story and what you’re putting out into the world. And so, when I watched [Thompson-Hernandez’s] short, I was like, ‘Yo, this is different. I ain’t never seen nothing like this.’ And it was captivating just the way he was shooting it.”.

Expanding on what drew her to the project, which came to her during her time bouncing between Los Angeles awards press for “The Color Purple,” and the New Zealand set of “A Minecraft Movie,” Brooks stated “They handed me the script and it was really the conversation, sitting down with Walter, his passion for his community, hearing about the real Lozita who had unfortunately passed away from cancer two years prior, hearing about the Compton Cowboys, just getting to talk to him about relationships between kids and their parents and the complications that it can bring.”.

It has been revealed that she stated, “I like the balance. I got to have a little comedy, but I got to do some drama and it does my heart well.” While “Minecraft” brought her “laughs all day with Jack Black and Jason Momoa,” “If I Go” brought Brooks “purpose.” “I’m excited that we get to share stories like this where people are really dealing with their personal concerns and healing and all of that stuff,” she said.

Having screened the film in Los Angeles the night before, Brooks said “You can feel the energy of everyone feeling super represented and feeling a sense of ownership. It’s cool hearing the audience be like, ‘Yeah, yeah,’ When you talk about the planes passing by, or the story about the fuel engines falling on elementary schools. People remember and know that to be a part of what has happened in LA, and the fabric of LA.”.

According to recent reports, one job that was foundational to how she approaches projects like “If I Go” happens to be Brooks’ breakout role as Taystee on “Orange Is the Newly introduced Black.” Coming out of the prestigious Julliard School, her mind was more so on “how am I going to make my money for the subway and pay for my college tuition and how am I going to pay for this PB&J sandwich?,” when she booked the role on the series for the then-nascent streaming service Netflix. “I didn’t know what I was stepping into at the time. ‘Orange’ was looked at as a webseries, so nobody knew what this was about to be. But once we got into the work, I was like, ‘Oh, this is deeper than that.’ I remember talking to people who’ve been incarcerated, and I remember even doing a clothing drive for women who have just come out of prison so that they could have clothes for job interviews and stuff like that. We were really invested in the community and giving back,” noted Brooks.

According to recent reports, “We had that as a group, as storytellers, but then individually, I was watching my co-stars have a point of view, have something to say. And so, I [was] just learning that being an artist is also a form of activism,” she mentioned. “That was one of the beginning seeds planted in my head once I was in the industry, because I’ve always known that what we do is about service, that’s number one. But I hadn’t experienced that on this level.”.

Since then, Brooks’ goal has been to tell at least one story a year that incorporates a bit of activism, and with “If I Go,” the actress and producer has been more active than ever. “I’ve deemed us the little engine that could, because I really believe that we can take this far. My goal is that we just get as many eyeballs on it as we can. But the truth of the matter is nothing moves like money does. And that’s what I’ve learned is you’ve got to get really creative and strategic about how you can push a movie into the face of the people when you don’t have the money.”.

Recent findings suggest that “If I Go Will They Miss Me,” distributed by Rich Spirit, has truly been an indie success story, making over $1 million at the box office from the humblest of beginnings. As Brooks noted, that haul has been hard fought, with her, Thompson-Hernandez, and her co-star J. Alphonse Nicholson touring as much of the country as they can to screen the film, and even abroad. “I’m going to Africa this week, I got invited, but then I learned there’s a film festival in Africa. So, I’m like, ‘Can we take the film to Africa?’ And they mentioned, ‘Yes.’ So now, the film’s going to be in the festival there,” said the actress.

Sources indicate that she continued, “It’s even in the form of fashion. People pay attention to what you’re wearing and then they’re like, ‘Why you got that on? Oh! She had a premiere.’ Boom. It’s insane how many tricks I have been working to get people to pay attention to this film that is worth paying attention to.”.

Recent findings suggest that one of the more beautiful aspects of this “If I Go” experience has been the way in which her community has shown up for her and the film. Snoop Dogg and Ava DuVernay have Instagrammed about it, while Helen Hunt and André Holland have even hosted talk backs for the film. But in terms of creativity, one marketing strategy takes the cake. “Issa Rae, even at her restaurant, she did a menu dedicated to ‘If I Go’ where it was a discount, 15 percent off or something if you bought a ticket,” she said. “People understand the importance of this,” said Brooks. “If the film wasn’t good, I wouldn’t be doing all this.”.

Industry observers note that on the awards front, the challenge is still getting the film in front of the steak eaters who still make up a good chunk of the awards body, and maybe do not immediately think they identify with the material. “The Academy is working really hard to change that narrative by who is allowed to vote. The voting party is shifting, but that’s what I’m experiencing right now,” said Brooks.

Sources indicate that but regular filmgoers have a role in getting smaller, truly independent films awards recognition too. “The general audience plays a huge part because the culture tells the voters where to look, what is notable,” mentioned the actress. “The people, we have a voice in this too. I think we make it very clear what we want to see, but it’s a weird cycle.” Studio films have a budget for billboards, commercials, advertisements, and more. “When you are a small independent film, you have to be that significant machine on your own to get it out there. And that’s a lot of work, and that’s a lot of time, and that’s a lot of smarts,” said Brooks. “You’ve got to have a lot of faith and hope too. You’ve just got to believe that what you’ve created is strong. And I do know that we all do, myself, J. Alphonse, Walter, MACRO, Rich Spirit, we believe in this film wholeheartedly.”.

Sources indicate that “Movies like these are worth telling, and I think they do reach who they need to reach, and they do lock in with the world on a larger scale when they’re supposed to,” stated Brooks, reflecting on the fruitful journey “If I Go” has already had so far. “This is the thing I’m most proud of in my whole career because just the fact that people are having conversations, hard conversations with their loved ones, and they’re finding ways to heal.”.

“If I Go Will They Miss Me” is now available to rent on all platforms.

CD Projekt Red is looking to bridge that gap with a fresh update.

In a recent development, CD Projekt Red released patch 5.02 on Nov. 26 across Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X. The revision includes a plethora of tweaks and bug fixes, such as fixing some recurring problems with Photo Mode, the main attraction is the expansion of the mod library. More than 40 upcoming cross-platform mods are now live, and more are on the way in the future.

According to recent reports, some of the highlights include "Glowing Witcher Eyes," a more lore-accurate depiction of Geralt that leans into the creepy nature of the Witchers. You can freshen up Geralt with a upcoming hairstyle or try out a boat race. The most impressive addition is the expansion-sized "Tales of the Witcher: Cintra," which adds a dozen quests. That should hold players over until Songs of the Past is released next year.

Witcher fans will be eating well in the next few years, as CD Projekt Red has several projects ​​​​​​​indevelopment​​​​​​​. The Witcher 3 expansion Songs of the Past will be released next year. The DLC​​​​​​​ is about the size of the 2016 expansion Blood and Wine and will serve as a finale to Geralt's adventures. A new trilogy of games starring Ciri will kick off in 2028 with The Witcher 4.

The Witcher multiplayer game Project Sirius got an encouraging update in November, when Baudelaire Welch joined the team as a senior writer specialist. They were responsible for the fan-favorite Dark Urge storyline in Baldur's Gate 3. Development of the Witcher 1 remake is at the moment on the back burner​​​​​​​ as the team waits for tools and assets from The Witcher 4.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that time is quickly running out to watch The Accountant 2 on streaming, as the R-rated action thriller starring Jon Bernthal and Ben Affleck is leaving a major service in a couple of days. The Accountant 2 originally came out in theaters in April 2025 courtesy of Amazon MGM and director Gavin O'Connor.

It has been revealed that nine years after the original thriller became a major hit, The Accountant 2 struggled to find as big an audience on the big screen. But it's since become a consistently strong performer on streaming services, starting on Prime Video before moving to other platforms. The Accountant 2 is rated R for strong violence and language throughout and has a 2-hour and 12-minute runtime.

If you're looking for a great action thriller, act fast before The Accountant 2 leaves streaming.

The Accountant 2 changed the formula of the first movie by becoming a buddy movie between Affleck and Bernthal. They reprised their roles from the first film as Christian Wolff, an autistic accountant and former assassin, and Braxton, his brother and active hitman. After only sharing a few scenes in The Accountant, the sequel leans all in on their chemistry.

It has been revealed that affleck and Bernthal have plenty of experience excelling in action thrillers, and they prove to be a terrific duo here. Bernthal gets to be a bit more flamboyant and charismatic, while Affleck plays things a bit more seriously. Together, they make The Accountant 2's buddy-style narrative really shine, bringing the film's action, drama, and humor to life really well.

It has been revealed that thanks to this approach, The Accountant 2 is a superior movie to the original. The first film had a solid relationship at its core between Affleck's character and Anna Kendrick's Dana Cummings, but its semi-romantic nature is absent from the sequel, allowing a brotherly bond to take center stage and go even bigger on the action.

Industry observers note that with Bernthal's elevated role, The Accountant 2 goes farther in its R-rating. That's the plus of having two trained killers at the heart of the story rather than just one. But The Accountant 2 works so well because it finds smaller moments to have fun, like Affleck dancing in a bar, and mixes in more comedy.

The plot can be a bit more ridiculous at times, especially with certain elements of The Accountant 2's ending, but there is a lot to like and enjoy overall. The sequel wound up scoring a 74% on Rotten Tomatoes with critics, but audiences adored the action-packed thriller, resulting in a 92% score. The Accountant has 53% and 77%, respectively.

It has been revealed that christian and Braxton's adventures aren't supposed to end with The Accountant 2, either. O'Connor confirmed years ago that he envisioned this story as a proper trilogy. He, Affleck, and screenwriter Bill Dubuque have teased The Accountant 3 being in development, but Amazon MGM has yet to give it an official green light.

Recent findings suggest that if The Accountant 3 does happen, it will bring Affleck and Bernthal back for another mission. O'Connor previously confirmed the threequel's intent to include Kendrick's return, too. Broader plot details have yet to be revealed, but the director described it as a road-trip movie bringing all three characters together.

While The Accountant 2 will leave Hulu on December 1, it should come to another streaming service eventually. It isn't listed among Prime Video's December 2026 movies, though, so when and where it will pop back up is unclear. Go watch it now while you still can.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s Note: The following review contains spoilers for “The Lowdown” Season 2 Episode 8, “The Tower” — including the finale’s ending.].

According to recent reports, “I saw the structure of the episode as these kind of waves that crash upon Lee,” Ethan Hawke stated in an interview about “The Lowdown‘s” Season 2 finale. “The way life works, it’s not like, ‘Oh, this one thing happens and then you change.’ It’s usually a series of things that happen, and the walls of your defenses come down.”.

Sources indicate that lee’s walls were certainly up when “The Lowdown” Season 2 began. Untethered by the acclaim for his Season 1 exposé on Dale Washberg (Tim Blake Nelson), Lee reacts with vehement defensiveness. He mocks the journalists who named him Tulsa’s Journalist of the Year during his acceptance speech. He alienates his friends and embarrasses his daughter. Related Stories ‘The Hunting Wives’ Review: Season 2 Reloads Without Slowing Down in Netflix’s Delirious Soap Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It.

He’s a mess, and when Ginger (Betty Gilpin) walks into his life with a tantalizing new story, he’s lucky — not because she’s the woman of his dreams carrying his drug of choice (a “truthstorian’s” next crusade), but because grounding forces are on the way in the form of his estranged father, Lee Raybon Sr. (Tommy Lee Jones), as well as a few clear-eyed, full-throated friends. Over the course of a riveting, revelatory Season 2, they all help to bring Lee back to himself, one wave at a time.

Industry observers note that the finale’s first swell comes as quite a surprise — two surprises, really. When Lee pulls up to the funeral home, prepared to pay a terse goodbye to his departed dad, so, too, does his former business partner and best friend, Wendell (played by Peter Dinklage). Wendell tells Lee he’ll “always be grateful” for Senior’s guidance when they were younger, and it’s immediately clear he’s not about to take the man’s final tribute as lightly as his son may have hoped.

“When Tommy’s character dies and there’s a funeral, we’re all like, ‘Well, wouldn’t Wendell be there?’ I mean, they’re really great friends,'” Hawke said. “I called Peter up and I was like, ‘Is there any way you’d come down for one day to be just at this funeral?’ And Peter was shooting in London and flew in and flew right back. He came in and made it happen for us.”.

Sources indicate that but Dinklage’s return was no mere cameo. Creator Sterlin Harjo knew better than to let the opportunity go to waste.

“I think there was a Shakespeare monologue in it first, and it was beautiful,” Harjo said. “Then Peter suggested the Dylan Thomas. […] I can’t imagine a more exciting way to have Peter be in your show than doing this Dylan Thomas poem that’s a gentle poem, but he does it with this rage — how it’s supposed to be read. It’s amazing.”.

Volunteering to speak when Ray (Michael Hitchcock) gets overwhelmed, Wendell spends a few seconds scrolling to find the right poem (“Do not go gentle into that good night”) and then tears into it with vigor. Dinklage’s recitation is more of a resuscitation — powerful enough to wake the dead, it wakes Lee up, snapping him into the present and bringing him back to life.

“When he’s doing the poem, he came in at a 10,” Harjo said. “The only direction I gave him was, ‘What if you build to that?’ And that’s what he did, and it was just unbelievably great.”.

Recent findings suggest that “That one is violent and abrupt,” Hawke noted. “It’s a friend shaking you up.”.

In Hawke’s case, Lee’s friend was his real friend. He knew Dinklage “loved poetry,” and he even knew a little bit about what his fellow actor would bring to this poem.

Recent findings suggest that “This is where collaboration is really mysterious about how it works and when it works really well,” Hawke said. “I’ve been friends with Peter Dinklage since, I don’t know, 1990. […] We both arrived in New York around the same time, and we used to sit around and tie one on and try to flirt with girls and read poems. We used to geek out about how much we loved the ways people would read poems in the old days. If you hear Dylan Thomas read a poem or you hear Orson Wells read a poem, they weren’t afraid of feeling or emotion or a theatricality. They weren’t afraid of passion — actual passion — and caring and looking foolish.”.

It has been revealed that “We’re living in an age of irony and cynicism and detachment, and this definition of cool being that you don’t care. Whereas the definition when I was growing up was Bob Marley and John Lennon and Miles Davis and those guys cared a tremendous amount. They weren’t detached. They were completely attached. So for me to watch Peter bring that to his performance was like, ‘Let me show you kids how to do a poem!’ [laughs] ‘You got to do it like your life depends on it.'”.

“The key to that scene is the interaction between him and Lee,” Harjo stated. “I love that he’s watching Lee the whole time. It’s like there’s no one else in the room and he’s doing it for Lee. I love that.”.

“The camera does pick up subconscious,” Hawke mentioned. “A lot of times I’ll see work that might be good, but it has no subconscious to it. I can tell there’s no secret sewn into the filmmaking. And Sterlin loves — you can call it poetry, you can call it whatever you want — but [he loves] when there’s multiple layers happening. […] And so for me, I’m not just sitting there with an actor doing this scene. I’ve known this guy for 30 years and I know what this poem means to him, and he knows me.”.

“If there was an Academy Award for Best Single Scene, I would give it to Peter Dinklage in our show.”.

While Dinklage may have to settle for an Emmy, Harjo had to write the other big finale monologue for an actual Oscar winner. At the reception, Lee’s daughter Francis (Ryan Kiera Armstrong) reads a passage from her grandfather’s journal, written shortly after Lee Jr. was born, as a way to honor her ancestor. Then, as Francis speaks Senior’s words, Senior appears seated behind her, and Tommy Lee Jones takes over the scene.

Sources indicate that “The bigger thing about that monologue is I knew it was coming,” Harjo noted. “I was like, ‘Oh shit, I got to write this thing for Tommy Lee Jones.’ I kind of had Tommy Lee Jones dialed in through the whole season. I felt like I could really write his voice. But when it came to that monologue, I’m like, ‘God, he’s already known for one of the best monologues in the world at the end of ‘No Country for Old Men,’ and I can either try to do a fancy monologue that isn’t like that at all, or I could lean into the fact that Cormac McCarthy and the Coen brothers did this really well already, and there’s no way that I don’t know that as a filmmaker. So I’m going to lean into it and almost give homage to that speech.'”.

“And that’s what I did. It has this bit of nostalgia. It also has this magic to it and this dreamlike quality to what he’s doing,” Harjo remarked. “The character is such an internal person that the only way you’re going to get those monologues is through a journal when he thinks it’s the privacy of himself and his journal. He’s expressing things that he wouldn’t normally express out loud.”.

Sources indicate that “Not to toot my own horn, but I feel like I nailed it,” he noted, laughing. “Of course, it filters through Tommy Lee Jones and all of a sudden it’s like this fucking amazing thing that he does. It was wonderful being on set. Just watching him give that, it was unbelievable. I could have used any take and it would’ve been amazing in a different way.”.

Throughout the monologue, Lee sits in thoughtful silence. He’s not only absorbing what his father wrote and remembering who he was; he’s also recognizing his shifting role as a son who’s now a father. There’s a connection across generations. Yes, his responsibility to his daughter means avoiding repeating his dad’s mistakes, which Lee is well-aware of, but it also means honoring his father’s better intentions, like the ones he voiced in that journal and Francis is voicing again now.

Sources indicate that “Lee’s adamant that he’s nothing like his father,” Hawke noted. “The first thought I had is, ‘All right, this is why Lee Raybon is obsessed with the truth: It’s that his father was a chronic liar.’ If you grew up in a house where your parent was really comfortable lying to you, you would get obsessed with people in power misleading you, and that would really drive you.”.

Sources indicate that “But then as we played the scenes deeper, I realized that Lee was lying to himself; that he was just as manipulative as his father is. He just does it in the name of truth. All this bad behavior that he was in denial of, he’d actually internalized it, and he was so much like his dad that he was completely blind to it, which is behavior I’ve seen in so many friends. It’s amazing. But I had to live through it. I didn’t get it when I was reading it. I got it when I was playing it, and that was very powerful for me.”.

Sources indicate that one way Harjo & co. illustrate Lee’s development over the course of Season 2 is simple: He listens. Instead of shouting, pontificating, or generally causing chaos, Lee spends much of the finale hearing what everyone around him has to say. Even when he’s up his own ass or annoying the hell out of folks, he has a community who cares about him, and their steady presence in his life is what eventually breaks down his defenses.

“The first [wave] is Peter reading that poem, and then the second one is gentle and persuasive where my daughter is revealing to me that my father did love me,” Hawke remarked. “Part of the thing you learn watching this show is that Lee feels like he has to conquer the world to be worthy of self-respect. His daughter is saying, ‘It’s right here for you, and it always has been.'”.

While another monologue played a significant role in how the episode plays out — Ginger’s speech to Francis, outside the bookstore — that moment wasn’t about Lee. (“The whole idea was Ginger and Francis don’t really get to hang out, but they are alike,” Harjo remarked. “Ginger immediately recognizes it and probably also knows that she had a father that was a lot like Lee.”) So his final wave comes from a curious source.

“The third one is just this final little moment that happens with Vickey (Abbie Cobb) when she tells him his fortune is bad and he sees it as a good thing. He understands that everything is point of view, and for him, towers coming down would be good.”.

“Those are the three steps that I think are designed to get Lee back on his feet again,” Hawke said. “That push him to be like, ‘All right, you know what? I’m not quitting. I’m going to keep being me, and I’m going to be a better version of me.'”.

How he’s feeling when Season 3 starts is anyone’s guess, and that assumes a renewal that’s yet to be unveiled is still in the offing from FX. But one thing’s for sure: If Lee comes back, he’ll be a changed man — and he won’t be alone.

“The Lowdown” is available on FX and Hulu.

STRAZZA: We're spoiled in Italy.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A security researcher has discovered a publicly exposed database containing approximately two billion credentials.
  • The scariest part of it is around 400,000 documents came from separate folders for individual victims, creating a detailed profile with all the personal data needed to “own that person” ….
  • Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler claims that the database contains a huge array of information, including login details for Tor .onion addresses used to access the dark web.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A security researcher has discovered a publicly exposed database containing approximately two billion credentials. The database was neither password-protected nor encrypted.

The scariest part of it is around 400,000 documents came from separate folders for individual victims, creating a detailed profile with all the personal data needed to “own that person” ….

Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler claims that the database contains a huge array of information, including login details for Tor .onion addresses used to access the dark web.

I also observed thousands of Tor .onion addresses associated with account names and passwords. The Tor .onion services are generally categorized as part of the dark web, and these credentials could potentially provide access to private forums, marketplaces, communication platforms, or other hidden services. While .onion accounts alone do not imply criminal or malicious activity, it is estimated that as much as 60% of dark web sites host illegal material and illicit activities. This is the first time I have seen a large number of dark web accounts in breached credentials. It should be noted that legitimate organizations, journalists, whistleblower platforms, and news organizations also operate .onion services to provide anonymity and bypass censorship.

But the most frightening aspect of it is separate folders for individual victims containing all of the information needed for identity theft.

Fowler told Wired that this data appears to have been obtained through advanced malware.

Industry observers note that the “scariest” thing in the database, Fowler indicates, was around 400,000 documents that appeared to come from “more advanced malware” compiling information about individual victims […] that create a detailed profile of an individual and their digital life. “If you had that, you own that person,” Fowler says.

It has been revealed that there’s no information about the specific sources of the data, but it seems likely to be aggregated from a range of data breaches. Fowler contacted the hosting tech giant to have the database removed, but it’s not known how many people may have had access to it.

The best protection is to use a password manager like Apple’s Passwords app to ensure you have strong, unique passwords for each individual website and service you use, with two-factor authentication enabled wherever possible. When given the choice of 2FA code delivery, you should always opt for an authenticator app rather than a text message to protect yourself against SIM-swap attacks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in September, Apple held a photography exhibition in New York City to show off the iPhone 18 Pro camera. Now, an image of the Bugaboo Mountains from that exhibit, shot by photographer Jimmy Chin, is included in TIME’s Top 100 Photos.

Sources indicate that TIME publishes its Top 100 Photos list each year. The list showcases the pictures that the TIME Photo Department determines best capture that particular year.

In a recent development, the essence of TIME’s Photos of the Year, selected by our photo editors and presented below, is the authentic, sometimes staggering, reality captured by photojournalism. Someone was there. A news photographer lifted a viewfinder, pressed a button, and captured an instant happening in front of them.

Chin’s image was shot in Bugaboo Provincial Park, Canada, on iPhone 18 Pro. He explained that a traditional production creates a layer of separation between the photographer and the subject, with equipment, crew, and all the moving parts of a shoot. Shooting on iPhone 18 Pro meant that he could create a more intimate environment, allowing for a sense of comfort and spontaneity that comes through in the images.

Image Courtesy of Apple (as featured in the What Holds Us exhibition).

Chin’s goal was to capture the intersection of human ambition and the pursuit of wonder against the backdrop of a timeless natural landscape.

“The resolution and the sharpness on iPhone 18 Pro surprised me. I could shoot a few inches of rock and ice, or a massive panorama, and trust it would hold at size. That is what this work needed. It also meant I carried almost nothing. In the mountains, everything you carry is a decision. I was not thinking about gear. I was thinking about what was in front of me.”.

Apple’s “What Holds Us” exhibit ran in Fresh York City in September, featuring work from photographers Alex Prager, Jack Davison, and Jimmy Chin, with each artist using the iPhone 18 Pro to explore the “people, places, and ideas that connect and ground humanity.” Kathy Ryan, the former longtime director of photography for The New York Times Magazine, curated the exhibition.

Sources indicate that the exhibit is now headed to London, where it will open to the public on December 4, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. It will also be open from Saturday, December 12 through Sunday, December 13, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

Industry observers note that [Editor’s note: This interview was originally published on April 24, 2026, when “I Swear” was released in American theaters. Aramayo recently won Best Actor in a Film at the BAFTA Scotland Awards. The film and his performance are eligible for this year’s Oscars, and “I Swear” is now streaming on Netflix.].

When Robert Aramayo signed on to play Scottish Tourette’s activist John Davidson in filmmaker Kirk Jones’ biopic “I Swear,” he could scarcely imagine where the film would take him.

A hit in the UK, the film netted Aramayo a pair of BAFTA wins earlier in the year, as the British actor won both the vaunted Rising Star Award (previous winners include James McAvoy, John Boyega, Tom Holland, Tom Hardy, and those are just some of its biggest names) and the Best Actor trophy (beating out Timothée Chalamet, Leonardo DiCaprio, Ethan Hawke, Jesse Plemons, and eventual Oscar winner Michael B. Jordan). Related Stories How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

But that’s hardly all that happened at the February awards show, which was instantly and forever marred by a number of loud, racist outbursts from Davidson himself that were directed at “Sinners” stars Jordan, Delroy Lindo, Wunmi Mosaku, and more. The fallout from the incident was both swift and prolonged, and will likely impact the domestic release of “I Swear,” which is rolling out in stateside theaters now.

Aramayo’s performance in the film is indeed star-making and awards-worthy, as he brings sensitivity and great courage to his portrayal of Davidson, following him from his earliest symptoms through his current passionate activism. Hopefully, viewers can see and appreciate the work on its own merits, and get to know Aramayo much better, though he has previously appeared in plenty of projects recognizable to American audiences, from “The Empty Man” to “The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” to a little thing called “Game of Thrones” (young Ned Stark!).

Ahead, Aramayo tells IndieWire about his deep research for the role, everything BAFTAs, and what he hopes will come from more people seeing the film and, hopefully, understanding Tourette’s all the better.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

It has been revealed that indieWire: When I saw the film at TIFF in September, I did my due diligence before I reviewed it, and learned that John is a huge figure in the UK, but relatively unknown in America. How much did you know about him before this film?

Recent findings suggest that robert Aramayo: John’s made a lot of documentaries, but the big one that probably had the most impact was “John’s Not Mad,” and that was in 1989. So if you speak to people who were around then, they have a lot of very personal stories about watching that documentary and being like, “Wow, is this Tourette’s? What’s Tourette’s?”.

So when you get the script, are you someone who then wants to do more research into him, or do you feel like the script is the thing?

Industry observers note that the production team and Kirk were so gracious, and they gave me so much time. I think they were like, “Oh, yeah, take a couple of months or something to research and stuff.” I was really thankful for that. The first thing that I did was to meet John; I met him very quickly. And then I went away for a month, and I spent that time gaining as much knowledge as I could about Tourette’s and what it is. That was through watching the documentaries, watching YouTube videos, and reading books.

I based myself in Galashiels and spent weeks with John, just following him around and spending as much time with him as I could. And also traveling through Scotland, meeting people, mainly through [support organization] Tourette Scotland, who lived with Tourette’s as well. I wanted to have, I don’t know, a more expansive view of Tourette’s than just John. Obviously, John was my main focus, though.

Industry observers note that when you’re getting ready to meet John, what were you expecting and anticipating? What were you nervous about?

I don’t know what I felt, really. I was so filled with anxiety about, oh my word, am I going to do this? I wanted John to like me. I was already feeling, God, this is going to be a really big challenge. And I met him within days of saying yes.

But then, when I met him, one thing that struck me straight away was his knowledge. He’s got a really amazing knowledge about, obviously, Tourette’s, but also a lot of neurodiversity and how it lives, other conditions that exist with Tourette’s, and stuff like that. He’s got a lot of thoughts about how we can do better and help young people and things like that. He’s very forthcoming with it.

In a recent development, he’s got so much heart. He’s such an amazing, welcoming, supportive man that I was just like, wow, this is a really impressive person that I’m meeting here. Of course, then your anxiety and the responsibility meter have gone through the roof.

According to recent reports, just watching the film, I learned so much about what Tourette’s can entail and the very wide spectrum of symptoms that people can have. What was the most unexpected thing you learned about it during your research?

Recent findings suggest that A couple of things really that had a really big impact on me straight away, and that sort of broke my perception of what I thought Tourette’s was, that anything can be a tic, and that it’s so singular to the person. So if you’ve met one person with Tourette’s, someone stated to me, you’ve met one person with Tourette’s. That was a big thing.

And also the fact that there’s a lot of tics that you just don’t see. There’s tics that you don’t see as tics because anything can be a tic, or there’s tics that exist only in somebody’s mind, and things like that, tics linked with OCD. Just the complexity of it was massive.

I learned some statistics recently, which I found really interesting: One in 50 kids in America live with persistent tic disorder, and one in 160 live with Tourette’s, so it’s unbelievably common, it’s everywhere. We have met people with Tourette’s, we meet them all the time. It was part of the experience of the film as well, we met loads of people who were living with Tourette’s undiagnosed. 50 percent of people who live with Tourette’s in the U.S. are undiagnosed, and that was true for us in the UK as well in our experience. Maybe the thing is that we don’t know that that’s what’s happening. That made me think, wow, there’s a real educational piece to this as well.

You are playing someone who is a real person who has been captured on film for many years. People know what he looks like, they know what he sounds like. How do you find the line between impersonation and impression in your performance?

Recent findings suggest that I never wanted to impersonate John. I think I would’ve gone the wrong way if that was what I was thinking. You have to, at a certain point, take ownership of the character and try and make him your own. I was lucky because there was so much that I needed to learn, so for so long, I wasn’t thinking about performance or playing him at all. I was just trying to immerse myself as much as I could in everything, anything that I could get my hands on. Then, at certain point, I moved to thinking about how I was going to try and play my version of John.

In a [narrative] film, you get the opportunity to maybe show a little bit more [than a documentary]. A documentary film crew comes into somebody’s life and they can capture what they can capture, but we could capture way more intimate moments throughout the whole film that John had spoken to.

We could show the moments where he is on his own, whether there’s been an impact or how he’s feeling or his emotional life, how things change over time and stuff like that, and hopefully try and do it with truth and authenticity.

You attended Juilliard, which always seems a little, “Oooohhh, he’s Juilliard-trained.”.

But now that you’re a few years out of school, what are the pieces of training that are proving to be most useful to you?

In a recent development, I think that acting teachers and drama school is vocabulary, really. At the time, certain things that teachers would say to me had a massive impact on me and really opened me up to other ways of looking at things, and other things are only impacting me now, as I keep working and as I get older. I think that’s the beauty of drama school, you get flooded with all of this stuff, and then you’re going, “Oh, that’s what they were talking about.” And then there’s things that my teachers would consistently say, “You’ve got to work on this, you’ve got to work on this,” and I’m still working on it. It’s like a toolbox, and every now and again you go, “Oh, yeah, that’s what I need.”.

They also made us do liberal arts which — I’m from Yorkshire, I don’t even know what liberal arts meant — but I’d encounter Nietzsche and Plato and all this stuff. I had no time at all to digest anything, but I’d read it and be like, “I don’t really know what’s going on here, but I think this is going to be important one day. I think I’m going to reread this one day!”.

What was the morning of the BAFTA nominations like for you?

I knew it was happening that morning. I remember talking to my agent, and we just didn’t speak about it, but we both knew that they were coming out that morning or whatever, so we had a really chill conversation about something else. [Laughs] I put it on in the background, because I thought we had a chance at, I don’t know, something, and then I heard that Peter had been nominated and I was so happy for him. I was elated for him.

Industry observers note that so, I was just in that, and I was doing the dishes, and I was like, “Wow, that’s so cool. I can’t wait to go text him.” And then they mentioned my name, and I just absolutely couldn’t believe it. My agent called me back straight away and was like, “Oh, my God.” It was an amazing feeling, but it was really unexpected because I was still really, really sort of overwhelmed by the Rising Star thing.

Industry observers note that you genuinely looked so surprised when you won Best Actor at the show. I feel like I would black out in that moment. Do you remember what that moment felt like?

Yeah, because I almost did! I had this weird physical reaction where I sort of went back [pantomimes sitting way back], and I think somebody grabbed me. I think I would’ve just kept going. I would’ve fallen off my chair or something.

According to recent reports, I honestly couldn’t believe it. I’m honestly not sure I still can believe that that’s something that happened to me, because for someone like me to be in that group of people blew my mind. I felt like, “Wow, and there I am, that’s my name.” To me, that was the thing that sort of really, really, really, really blew me away. When it happened, yes, it all just becomes a blur, and I’m running down the stairs, and I don’t know what the hell I’m going to say.

According to recent reports, obviously, other things happened at the awards show involving John. As someone who had seen the film, I felt like I had a greater grasp on what was happening; I had that context. Now that the film is coming out in America, what hopes do you have for people seeing the film and how that might impact that conversation?

It has been revealed that I think lots of people watch the film, and they feel like their education around Tourette’s has improved and increased, and that would be amazing [if that continued]. I think it’s crucial to acknowledge that … Tourette’s has an impact on a person who’s ticcing, and the same tic obviously has an impact on the person who’s receiving the tic or impacted by the tic. And it’s important to acknowledge that, because that is what it is. Coprolalia, which is the tic that John has, that tic, it’s not saying what you think, it’s saying the worst thing imaginable. That’s how it was described to me.

Sources indicate that I hope people watch the film. And I hope people watch the film and think, “Oh, I’ve learned something about Tourette’s.” I hope that people watch the film from the community, because that’s been an amazing thing as well. People watching it who have lived with Tourette’s or lived with another neurodiverse condition have reached out and stated, “I see myself in this.” You want people to go to the movies and enjoy the film, but if people go home and Google “John Davidson” or Google “Tourette’s,” that’d be amazing.

In a recent development, the film is going to introduce you to a much larger audience, but you’ve also been in some massive hits before this one. Which is a fun way to ask: Do you know that “The Empty Man” has a huge cult fandom?

[Laughs] I’ve been told this. What an experience. I loved making that film. It was a long journey with it, and I learned a lot. And it was my first movie that I’d done with James Badge Dale, and I did another one with him as well. And I really, really liked working with him. He’s a really nice guy, and he’s a really talented actor. And the director, David [Prior], was wonderful. I learned a lot on that film. I love that people love that film.

In a recent development, you are also in the “Lord of the Rings” world as well. Are you going to be turning out to see “The Hunt for Gollum”?

Recent findings suggest that I’m so excited. I can’t wait. I’m a massive fan of the Peter Jackson films. I can’t wait to see what they do with it. It’s a really interesting story. I’m glad that they’re doing it and doing it properly.

Now that you’ve had what feels like a big breakthrough, what sort of things are you pursuing next?

Sources indicate that what do I want to do next? I don’t know! I feel lucky to just be an actor, to work. I’ve been lucky enough to work with some incredible people on “I Swear,” to work with Kirk and Peter and Shirley and Maxine. People like that, you learn, you grow, you get better. And so if I can just keep doing it, I’ll be happy.

That Rising Star Award feels like a lot of pressure!

In a recent development, I just feel really, really grateful for everyone who voted for me. It’s such a cool award that the public, the British public, vote for you. I feel so grateful for everyone who voted for me. I just feel very, very grateful for the whole thing, for everything, and mainly that people hopefully watch the film and talk about it.

CAD images of the iPhone 18e, remarked to come from a previously reliable source, have shown a rather odd new design for the camera bump.

If accurate, it would represent a major change from its predecessor, which simply has a single lens protruding without a surrounding bump or plateau ….

Sources indicate that the iPhone 17e was launched in March with a design unchanged from last year’s iPhone 16e. While the camera did get some feature enhancements, including the ability to store depth information for portrait photos, the physical camera design remained the same.

In a recent development, the current model has a single lens protruding directly from the casing with a flush-mounted flashlight next to it. Engadget reports on CAD images showing a very different approach with next year’s iPhone 18e.

The renders show an almost square camera bump measuring about 28 mm by 35 mm that houses the single rear camera, the LED flash and the rear microphone.

The site doesn’t share the images, but says that the camera bump looks similar to that of the M5 iPad Pro, shown below.

It’s unclear what might have prompted the change of design, especially as the site’s Filipe Espósito states he’s also seen CAD models for the standard model iPhone 18 or the iPhone Air 2, neither of which adopt it.

Previous reports have suggested that the only spec change with the iPhone 18e over its predecessor will be performance improvements thanks to the A20 chip.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nathan Fillion may not be leading any giant blockbusters at the box office, but he’s been in plenty of projects in the last few years with large audiences. One of Fillion’s biggest hits that immediately comes to mind is The Rookie, the ABC cop drama in which he plays John Nolan and has for almost 10 years. The next season of The Rookie is set to kick off early next year on ABC, which leaves fans plenty of time to catch up on past seasons on Hulu. Fillion’s DCU role as Guy Gardner’s Green Lantern is now up in the air following the news that James Gunn and Peter Safran had been replaced as the CEOs of DC by Jeremy Latcham, who spent years working on the Marvel machine with Kevin Feige.

Recent findings suggest that nathan Fillion is also widely known and loved for his roles in older demonstrates, such as Castle, another ABC series that was on the air for seven years in the late 2000s and early 2010s. However, even before Castle, Fillion starred in the first and only season of the hit sci-fi series that’s gone on to become a cult-classic in the last 20 years, Firefly. Other names involved in the show include Morena Baccarin, Alan Tudyk, and even Adam Baldwin, and the show was written and created for TV by Joss Whedon, who directed The Avengers and Avengers: Age of Ultron. Earlier this year, news broke that an animated Firefly reboot is officially in the works after 20 years, but it’s still unclear at this time when it will be released. However, Fillion recently went on the Revenge Of podcast with Patton Oswalt, and he shared an update about how things are going on the project:.

According to recent reports, “Listen, things happened, albeit very slowly. But, things are still moving forward. Not in the way I thought it would, but in more ways, yes, I’m getting more yeses than I am nos, which is wonderful.”.

The first and only season of Firefly, which consists of 14 episodes, can be streamed in its entirety on either Prime Video or Hulu in America. The first season of Firefly holds a solid 77% from critics on the aggregate site Rotten Tomatoes, but it’s on the audience-driven Popcornmeter where the show really shines, as it holds a near-perfect 96%. Even on IMDb, Firefly holds an 8.9 rating out of 10, which comes from over 300,000 reviews. It’s safe to say that expectations for the reboot are high.

Check out all episodes of Firefly on Hulu or Prime Video and stay tuned to Collider for more updates and coverage of the animated reboot series.

The Super Mario Galaxy Movie (2026).
