📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, upgrading your TV's sound doesn't necessarily mean spending a fortune on a full home theater setup, especially with early Black Friday deals bringing substantial discounts on soundbars and audio systems from Sony, Bose, Samsung, and LG. Sony has some of the biggest price cuts, with savings of up to 32% across select Bravia Theater models, including more than $700 off its premium Theater Trio system.

According to recent reports, samsung's Dolby Atmos soundbars are also discounted by as much as $400, while Bose and LG have more affordable options for anyone looking to improve dialogue clarity, add some bass, or enjoy surround sound without a complicated setup. Whether you're shopping for a compact speaker for a bedroom TV or a more immersive system for movie nights, here are the deals worth considering.

For anyone building a premium home theater around a large TV, the Sony Bravia Theater Trio is down to $1,498 from $2,199.99, saving you $701.99, or roughly 32%. Unlike a conventional soundbar, the Trio uses three separate front speakers for the left, center, and right channels, helping spread dialogue and effects across a wider soundstage. You can read PCMag’s “excellent” review for more details.

Recent findings suggest that the Sony Bravia Theater Bar 7 is down to $718 from $869 for anyone who wants a single soundbar under the TV. Its nine speakers include upward- and side-firing drivers that widen the soundstage and give Dolby Atmos some height, but there’s no subwoofer, so the now $898 Bar 7 with a wireless sub bundle (down from $1,099.99) might be the better pick for deeper bass.

Recent findings suggest that moving down Sony's lineup, the Bravia Theater Bar 6 is $548, down from $699.99, and pairs a 3.1.2-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer and upward-firing speakers for Dolby Atmos height effects. Spending $100 more gets you the Bravia Theater System 6, now $648 from $799.99, which adds rear speakers in a 5.1-channel setup for movies and games where sound moves behind you.

For a more affordable upgrade, the Sony Bravia Theater Bar 5 is down to $278 from $349.99, saving you nearly $72. It's a 3.1-channel system with a dedicated center speaker and wireless subwoofer, so dialogue should come through more clearly while music and movie effects get some additional low-end presence.

Industry observers note that sony’s older systems are discounted too, including the HT-S400 at $258, down from $299, which pairs a 2.1-channel soundbar and wireless subwoofer with S-Force Pro Front Surround to widen the sound for everyday TV, sports, and casual movies. The HT-S40R is arguably the better deal at the same $258, down from $329.99, since it adds two rear speakers for a full 5.1-channel setup, though neither model supports Dolby Atmos.

It has been revealed that for smaller rooms or for anyone who mainly wants dialogue to come across more clearly, Bose has two compact soundbars on sale: The newer Bose TV Speaker (2nd Gen) is down to $239 from $299, with an updated acoustic design that Bose says improves clarity and overall sound performance. Meanwhile, the original Bose TV Speaker is $199, down from $279, and offers a similarly compact design with a dedicated dialogue mode and adjustable bass.

It has been revealed that samsung’s HW-Q800H is down to $697.99 from $1,097.99, a $400 cut on a 5.1.2-channel Dolby Atmos soundbar with a wireless subwoofer. Its side- and upward-firing speakers help place effects around and above you, while a dedicated center channel keeps dialogue clear during busy action scenes.

For something that takes up less space, the Samsung HW-S60D is $277.99, down from $399.99, and fits seven speakers, including side-firing drivers, into a compact 5.0-channel soundbar. It also supports Dolby Atmos, Adaptive Sound, and a voice enhancement mode, along with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, AirPlay, and Chromecast for music streaming. That said, it has no upward-firing speakers or subwoofer, so its height effects and bass won’t match that of the Q800H.

If you're looking for a complete surround sound system without spending several hundred dollars, the LG S6FTR is down to $249.99 from $399.99, saving you $150, or roughly 38%. It's a 5.1-channel home theater package with a soundbar, subwoofer, and dedicated rear speakers. That makes it particularly appealing for action movies and games, where directional sound adds to the experience.

The LG S40TR is another affordable option for anyone who wants rear speakers included in the box. It's currently $199.99, down from $279.99, and offers a 4.1-channel arrangement with a wireless subwoofer and two rear speakers. This should give movie soundtracks a greater sense of direction than a basic soundbar, while the subwoofer handles the lower frequencies that smaller TV speakers often struggle to reproduce.

It has been revealed that at just under $187, the S60T is the least expensive system in this roundup, pairing a 3.1-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer for clearer dialogue and fuller sound than your TV’s speakers. That said, it lacks rear speakers and Dolby Atmos height channels, so it’s better suited to someone who wants a simple, affordable upgrade without filling the room with additional hardware.

Sources indicate that in short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Sources indicate that black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

Last year, Apple officially unveiled CarPlay Ultra, the next-generation version of CarPlay that it first teased way back at WWDC 2022.

Industry observers note that carPlay Ultra first released for Aston Martin owners in the United States and Canada. What about other automakers? Here’s what we know.

9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

Updated November 24, 2026: Latest on Hyundai, more.

In December 2023, Apple mentioned that Porsche and Aston Martin would be the first automakers to support next-generation CarPlay starting in 2024. That deadline came and went, and Apple confirmed in January that next-gen CarPlay had been delayed but was still in development.

Industry observers note that apple doesn’t offer a timeline on when CarPlay Ultra will actually be available through any other brand beyond Aston Martin. The company also does not have a dedicated list of automakers that have signed on to support CarPlay Ultra listed on its website.

Sources indicate that when Apple confirmed the next-generation version of CarPlay at WWDC 2022, however, it stated that several brands had committed to supporting the platform. In May of last year, Apple touted that three new partners had signed on: Hyundai, Kia, and Genesis.

However, several brands have also dropped their plans to support CarPlay Ultra. Mercedes-Benz was originally on Apple’s list, but abandoned its plans to support next-generation CarPlay in 2024. According to the Financial Times, Audi, Volvo, Polestar, and Renault have also decided against supporting CarPlay Ultra, despite originally being touted as partners by Apple.

With all of that said, here is the full list of automakers who blueprint to eventually support CarPlay Ultra, as of November 2026.

What do we know beyond this list? Not a whole lot. Interestingly, Top Gear reported that the Hyundai IONIQ 3 EV would support CarPlay Ultra. Hyundai announced the IONIQ 3 in April, but has not commented on whether the vehicle will support CarPlay Ultra as rumors suggested.

Mark Gurman at Bloomberg has also reported CarPlay Ultra will launch for “least one major new Hyundai/Kia model in the second half of this year.”.

While Apple has touted Ford as a partner for CarPlay Ultra, the automaker recently signaled it’s not too impressed with the first version of a platform.

Industry observers note that in a recent interview, Ford CEO Jim Farley was asked whether the manufacturer is “considering” CarPlay Ultra support. Here’s what he said:.

In a recent development, “We are. We don’t like the execution in round 1 of Ultra, but we’re very committed to Apple. I’ve talked to Tim many times about this.”.

It’s better than a flat “no,” but perhaps not the enthusiasm Ford drivers might have hoped to hear.

The question at this point is whether any other automakers have ditched CarPlay Ultra. Ideally, Apple will provide a full list sooner rather than later, but in the meantime, this is the only information we have.

AWOL Vision’s Black Friday deals include UST (ultra-short-throw) and long-throw models, but what’s the difference?

An ultra-short-throw projector, like the Aetherion models, is positioned close to the wall, with no ceiling mount or unsightly cables across the room, making it an ideal choice for living areas like a lounge or bedroom.

Sources indicate that conversely, long-throw projectors like the Valerion models on offer here are more cinema-like, sitting at the back of a room or being suspended from a ceiling mount. That makes it perfect for dedicated theater or media rooms.

Regardless of which option you opt for, AWOL Vision’s projector models offer 4K resolution, RGB triple laser for a wider color gamut, Dolby Vision, and are IMAX Enhanced.

The Aetherion lineup is AWOL Vision’s premier UST option for bringing the cinema to your home.

The AWOL Aetherion Max offers 3,300 ISO lumens of brightness and 6,000:1 native contrast ratio for daytime viewing in well-lit rooms, as well as 110% Rec.2020, with PixelLock™ Technology for sharp 4K images up to 200”.

It delivers 2,600 ISO lumens, 6,000:1 native contrast and 110% Rec.2020, with PixelLock™ Technology for sharp 4K images up to 200", and is now under $2,000 at $1,999 (discounted by 43% from the standard price of $3,499).

According to recent reports, apple Home is kicking off a new era with Siri AI-driven products like HomeView, making it a great time to upgrade your smart home with Apple Home-compatible accessories. Here are my top five picks.

Sources indicate that iOS 27 upgraded Apple’s HomeKit Secure Video service (included with iCloud+) in several key ways. You’ll now get searchable videos, highlighted clips, 4K support, and more.

I have two recommendations for HomeKit Secure Video-compatible cameras. The main difference is video quality, and whether they’re designed for outdoor use or only indoors.

Smart locks have always offered convenience, but with the advent of Ultra Wideband-supported locks, they’re better than ever.

In a recent development, aqara’s U400 smart lock was among the first to introduce Ultra Wideband, which enables your door to lock and unlock automatically when it senses your presence. Unlike prior smart lock automations that relied on Bluetooth, Ultra Wideband offers excellent reliability and precision for a great overall experience.

Sources indicate that want to open your garage door with a quick Siri command, or via CarPlay or the Home app on iPhone? Smart garage door openers with Apple Home support can deliver that, and my recommendation is the meross MSG150HK.

meross says the MSG150HK is compatible with “the vast majority of Chamberlain, Lift-Master, and Craftsman brand openers.” And it supports security features like automatic notifications when your door is left open, or every time it opens and closes.

Industry observers note that smart plugs are often a gateway to building out a smart home. And my favorite option, both for cost and convenience, is Tapo’s multipack of smart plugs.

It has been revealed that tapo sells its smart plug in a 2-pack at a great price—right now only $8 per plug. These plugs are compact and offer seamless, quick setup through the Home app without needing a separate app.

According to recent reports, controlling your thermostat entirely from your iPhone or a HomeView can prove extremely convenient. That convenience can also save you money by making it easier to stay on top of your electricity usage.

Aqara’s W200 smart thermostat is a beautifully designed, easy-to-use accessory that comes with a bonus Apple feature that’s hard to find: Adaptive Temperature, which can remove lots of the need to manually enhancement the thermostat.

What are your top Apple Home accessory recommendations? Let us know in the comments.

Walmart’s early Black Friday sale just kicked off, offering no shortage of worthy tech deals, and one home audio deal in particular has our attention. If you’re looking to level up your home theater audio setup for less, the Vizio 4.1 Pro SV410YW-10 Soundbar and wireless surround speakers setup with Dolby Atmos and DTS:X support is on sale for $79 (originally $148), a nearly 50% discount.

It has been revealed that the two pre-paired wireless surround speakers can be positioned behind or beside your seating area, while two bass drivers built into the 32-inch soundbar mean you don’t need a separate subwoofer. The system maxes out at 95 dB, with bass extending to 50 Hz.

The SV410YW-1 connects to your television through HDMI eARC and supports CEC, so you can adjust the volume with your TV remote. While its integrated subwoofers won’t give you the same impressive low end as a dedicated unit, this system still delivers robust, bassy sound that goes far beyond built-in TV speakers. There’s an added perk for Vizio TV owners—it can be attached directly beneath the screen using the QuickFit feature.

Recent findings suggest that along with the deal are additional promos, like up to two free months of Apple Music and up to a free month of Apple TV. If your current TV sound setup is lacking some oomph and you want an under-$100 upgrade with a subwoofer and soundbar, the Vizio 4.1 Pro SV410YW-10 Soundbar and wireless surround speaker combo is a good choice for the money.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scroll through Amazon for five minutes and you’ll find dozens of $10–20 cases that look, through a thumbnail, almost identical to $50+ aramid fiber ones. Same dark weave, same slim profile, same pitch.

Once you actually snap one onto a phone, the differences are obvious. You handle your phone for hours every day, so rough seams around the charging port, awkward cutouts, low-quality materials will make you regret your purchase instantly. With PITAKA’s Black Friday sale taking up to 30% off selected cases, it’s worth breaking down what actually separates a real aramid case from a cheap lookalike, why you should spent the extra money on PITAKA’s high-quality cases.

This post is sponsored by PITAKA.

Industry observers note that plenty of budget cases get the woven look by printing a pattern onto plain plastic. If you’re looking for that style, go for it, but it won’t behave like woven aramid fiber, which lets a case stay rigid and thin without adding much weight.

Recent findings suggest that even genuine aramid cases aren’t all made the same way. The weave, resin, thickness, and surface finish all change how a case feels in use. PITAKA uses woven aramid fiber in two main weights: 600D and 1500D. Those numbers measure yarn density; the finer 600D weave feels a bit smoother and produces a slightly thinner shell than 1500D. Whatever case you choose, look past the word “premium” and check whether the maker actually spells out what the case is made of.

Most aramid cases stick to plain black and gray. PITAKA’s Fusion Weaving method blends colored fibers and multiple weave styles directly into the shell instead of printing a graphic on the outside. PITAKA states the process requires tight control over fabric tension and how fibers cross between layers. In practice, it means you can pick something colorful like the Sunset colorway without giving up the feel of woven fiber, or stick with classic Black & Grey if you prefer a quieter look.

In a recent development, online listings spend almost all their time showing off the back of a case, even though your fingers spend just as much time on the sides, buttons, and bottom edge. An awkward camera cutout makes quick shots annoying, a tight port opening fights bulkier charging cables, and sharp edges dig into your hand on a long call.

Rather than selling one shell in ten colors, PITAKA splits its lineup into three builds:.

If you use a magnetic charger, wallet, or grip, how the magnets are built into the case matters just as much as the outer material. Sticking a separate magnet ring inside a shell usually adds extra layers and thickness.

In a recent development, PITAKA’s Amber Magnet Film process bonds coated magnets directly with the aramid fiber and resin under heat and pressure. That keeps the magnets enclosed without bulking up the case, which is the kind of detail you won’t spot in a photo but will notice in your pocket.

Recent findings suggest that spending more on a case doesn’t guarantee it’s better, and plenty of $20 cases are completely fine. Genuine aramid fiber by itself doesn’t guarantee better drop protection either. A thin shell like Edge is made for people who hate bulky cases. If drop protection is your main concern, look at a cushioned option like Cairn or Summa, and compare actual edge coverage and model-specific testing instead of judging by price or material alone.

What you’re really paying for with a higher-end aramid case is how it feels and fits every time you pick up your phone.

If you already want a thinner, better-finished case, Black Friday takes some of the sting out of the price. PITAKA’s Amazon offers run November 19–30, with discounts varying by device and colorway:.

Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2920 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The AI pioneer indicates it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to significant challenges.
  • Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.
  • Sources indicate that andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The AI pioneer indicates it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to significant challenges.

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Sources indicate that andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he says he has identified the next major shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

It has been revealed that ng’s current efforts are focused on his organization Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he states can yield “small data” solutions to big complications in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

The great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

Industry observers note that andrew Ng: This is a significant question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having said that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

It has been revealed that ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a latest paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

It has been revealed that ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Sources indicate that having noted that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of users, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing manufacturer with millions of consumers.

Industry observers note that ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

In a recent development, “In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from massive data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI.

It has been revealed that I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and remarked, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

I expect they’re both convinced now.

According to recent reports, over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing newly introduced here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”.

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Sources indicate that ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and said, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

It has been revealed that the data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one organization or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that showed up.

In a recent development, you often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Recent findings suggest that ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

When you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand newly introduced model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

In a recent development, ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having mentioned that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For big data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng.

According to recent reports, for example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very swiftly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

Ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. New tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an key piece of the puzzle.

One of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Recent findings suggest that ng: In AI, data cleaning is important, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention quickly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

It has been revealed that for example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

It has been revealed that ng: I think synthetic data is an crucial tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

According to recent reports, ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

“In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng.

In a recent development, synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

To make these issues more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a company approaches Landing AI and says it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

In a recent development, ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

One of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

How do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

It has been revealed that ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift issue. I find it really vital to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and revision the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion customers. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

It has been revealed that ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent fresh neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s key for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

Industry observers note that ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print glitch as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AirTag 2 (now only $18, down from $29) launched earlier this year after a five-year wait, and in my experience there are two significant improvements that make it worth the upgrade.

Precision Finding is Apple’s best AirTag feature, letting you get step-by-step, highly precise directions to your lost item. But with the original AirTag, you had to be in fairly close proximity before you could benefit from Precision Finding.

Industry observers note that with AirTag 2, Apple added a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip that makes Precision Finding now available from up to 1.5x farther away than before. It’s a huge increase that I’ve definitely noticed.

This expansion of Precision Finding to greater distances means the feature is now available a lot more often than with the old AirTag. For this reason alone, I highly recommend AirTag 2.

According to recent reports, when you’re trying to find a lost item, Precision Finding isn’t the only tool AirTag offers. There’s also a built-in speaker that can play a sound, triggered by your iPhone, to help you track it down.

It has been revealed that with AirTag 2, Apple has made the built-in speaker 50% louder than before. The company notes this enables hearing it from up to twice as far away.

I’ve been impressed by how loud the AirTag speaker is able to get now. Between the upcoming speaker and upgraded Precision Finding, Apple has made AirTag 2 better in the ways that people are likely to care about most.

You can buy AirTag 2 for $18 on Amazon (regularly $29) for a limited time.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the Asics Gel-Nimbus 29 swaps in a latest midsole foam to deliver a more comfortable and softer ride than its predecessors, and it’s a better easy-run cruiser as a result.
  • Industry observers note that why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you.
  • The Asics Gel-Nimbus 29 is almost three decades old, and to celebrate, Asics has made the biggest update to the shoe we’ve seen in years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Asics Gel-Nimbus 29 swaps in a latest midsole foam to deliver a more comfortable and softer ride than its predecessors, and it’s a better easy-run cruiser as a result. However, the new foam is so soft that the Gel-Nimbus 29 is a bit limited compared to bouncier cushioned shoes like the Asics Novablast 6 or Nike Vomero Plus.

Industry observers note that why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The Asics Gel-Nimbus 29 is almost three decades old, and to celebrate, Asics has made the biggest update to the shoe we’ve seen in years.

It has been revealed that A newly introduced midsole foam is at the heart of the changes, with the FF Luxe Plus material introduced in the Asics Slowcush being rolled down to the Gel-Nimbus 29. It’s a very soft foam and transforms the ride of the Gel-Nimbus 29 compared to past models.

Overall, I rate the latest Nimbus as an upgrade, and the softer ride makes its role clearer in the Asics line-up compared with the more versatile Asics Novablast 6, but the ride did sometimes stray into too-soft territory for my taste.

Industry observers note that the Asics Gel-Nimbus 29 launched in October 2026 and costs $170 in the U.S. and £170 in the U.K., which is the same price as the Gel-Nimbus 28 in the U.S., while in the U.K. the price has actually gone down by £10.

However, right now you can get the Asics Gel-Nimbus 28 for $129 in Amazon’s sale, and the older shoe is likely to remain around that price now that the newly introduced model is out.

The Asics Gel-Nimbus 29 is presently available in 10 colors for the men’s shoe and 11 for the women’s, and you can pick between wide and standard fits.

I actually tested a full size down from my normal running shoe size by accident, so it did come up a little tight as you’d expect, but I think going with your normal size will be fine.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The Gel-Nimbus 29 is a max-cushioned shoe and keeps the same stack height as its predecessor, standing 43.5mm tall at the heel and 35.5mm at the forefoot for an 8mm drop.

It’s a little lighter than the previous model, though, and weighs 9.7oz in my US men’s size 9, which is pretty light for such a cushioned shoe.

The Gel-Nimbus 29 has an engineered mesh upper that prioritizes comfort over being lightweight, and it is comfortable thanks to soft, stretchy material and padding around the collar.

I do like that the tongue isn’t overly padded, though, because this makes it feel a bit lighter and less oppressive — the tendency with highly cushioned shoes like this is to also max out the padding on the upper, which I find can make them hot and sweaty at times.

The past four generations of the Gel-Nimbus used FF Blast Plus foam in their midsoles (or the plant-based variant FF Blast Plus Eco), and although the exact makeup and feel of this foam did change between models, they have a similar ride.

You can definitely notice the difference with the introduction of FF Luxe Plus foam in the Gel-Nimbus 29, which still also retains a small slab of PureGel under the heel.

It’s a softer shoe, with a little more bounce than its predecessor as well, and it’s also softer than the Novablast 6 and Gel-Cumulus 28.

Another small enhancement to the Gel-Nimbus 29 is found on its outsole, which has more extensive rubber coverage than past models.

The Hybrid AsicsGrip material has gripped well on slick sidewalks during the British autumn and highlights no signs of wear and tear after 35 miles.

I’ve tested every version of the Gel-Nimbus since the 24, and while there have been minor updates in each of the past few years, it’s been a pretty similar experience since FF Blast Plus was introduced with the Gel-Nimbus 25.

That’s not to say it’s been a bad experience, but it's been the same and not all that remarkable when looking around the market, which is full of max-cushioned cruisers.

The Asics Gel-Nimbus 29 does stand out a lot more, both from past models and when compared to other brands’ top-cushioned options, just because it is so soft.

From my first step in the shoe, I could feel myself sinking into the FF Luxe Plus midsole, which is great for delivering a comfortable ride and absorbing the shock of running.

However, it’s not the most responsive foam — the Gel-Nimbus 29 is all about comfort and less about rebound, based on my testing.

On easy runs under an hour long, it felt great, but when I ran at faster paces or did a long run in the Gel-Nimbus 29, the foam started to feel like it was sapping energy rather than bouncing it back.

According to recent reports, this is not a versatile shoe like the Novablast 6, which is comfortable but also lively at faster paces. The Gel-Nimbus is a shoe that works very well for easy efforts, but I’d pair it with a faster, firmer shoe for workouts in a running shoe rotation.

If you love a soft running shoe, the Asics Gel-Nimbus 29 is one of the softest I’ve tried, and it’s certainly a comfortable pick for racking up the miles.

It’s actually a little too soft for my preferences; I’d rather use the firmer, more responsive Novablast 6 or bouncier Nike Vomero Plus for daily training, but I’m sure many runners will love the feel of the Gel-Nimbus 29.

Given its high price, I'd also be tempted to look at cheaper cushioned options, though, like the Kiprun Kipride Max or Hoka Clifton Pro, which both have smoother rides and more energetic foams in their midsole.

I’ve not tested the Asics Slowcush myself, but given it uses an even higher stack of the FF Luxe Plus foam found in the Gel-Nimbus 29, I’m sure it would be a good alternative for those chasing the softest ride possible.

The changes to the Gel-Nimbus 29 were long overdue, though, and I think it now stands out more as a premium cushioned option, both within the Asics line-up and when compared to rivals from other brands.

You can tell that Miranda Lambert is from Texas, but, until today, she’d never performed for her hometown football team — or anyone in the NFL, for that matter. Singing a medley of her classic hits (which she affectionately called “bangers and mash,” i.e., a mashup of her bangers), Lambert made her halftime show debut during the Thanksgiving Day matchup between the Dallas Cowboys and the Philadelphia Eagles at AT&T Stadium.

According to recent reports, following a pretaped introduction by Reba McEntire, who confirmed Lambert as the “most awarded artist in the history of the Academy of Country Music,” the Grammy-winning singer took the stage to perform “Snakeskin Boots” (sorry, no Ella Langley cameo), “Kerosene,” “Gunpowder & Lead,” “Mama’s Broken Heart,” and “Little Red Wagon.” Lambert was backed by her band, along with a string section wearing black cowboy hats to mirror that of the entertainer: Lambert, in a black hat, wore a black dress adorned with blue fames. She also received an assist from an army of Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders, who delivered their choreographed routine as Lambert sang.

Recent findings suggest that lambert is a lifelong Cowboys fan who grew up in Lindale, Texas, about 80 miles east of Dallas. She now joins a cast of music’s biggest names as a halftime show veteran, including Beyoncé, Reba McEntire, LeAnn Rimes, Lainey Wilson, and Dolly Parton, who gave a memorable performance while wearing the iconic Dallas Cowboy Cheerleaders costume. Coined the “Salvation Army’s 30th Red Kettle Kickoff,” it was McEntire who performed at the inaugural broadcast, which kicks off the annual holiday fundraising drive. Lambert, true to form, announced her appearance from atop a longhorn bull. In a recent development, black Friday is usually a great time to grab a new e-reader, but the ongoing RAM crisis has made that a question mark this year: Amazon recently raised the prices of all its Kindles by around $50 and refreshed the entire lineup, which means your odds of grabbing one at a significant discount are low. But you aren't totally out of luck: If you haven't noticed, micro-e-readers—I'm talking credit card-sized, with screens that measure around four inches—are all the rage in 2026, and right now, you can pick up one of them for around $55.

If you too can see the appeal of carrying all of your books with you on a device so small you'll forget it's even in your pocket, it's a great time to jump in: The recently released Xteink X4 Classic is currently 38% off for Black Friday, bringing it down to $54.87, a record-low price. Meanwhile, the smaller X3 is $55.72, or 19% off. Both are available in either "mist grey" or "space black." The discounts should last through the end of Cyber Monday on Nov. 30.

Sources indicate that xteink is a Chinese startup that shook up the e-reading world last year with the launch of the X4, a super bare-bones device that made up for its lack of features and usability with a cheap sub-$70 price point. Since then, a huge online community of fans has formed, sharing tips on Reddit and even coming together to crowdsource an alternate operating system that fixed a lot of early problems. Xteink rapidly followed up the X4 with a slate of other devices, including the 3.7-inch X3 and the X4 Pro, which adds a front light and touchscreen (at the cost of screen clarity and two physical buttons).

Sources indicate that the X4 Classic and the X3 improve on the original X4 with quality-of-life upgrades like a larger battery, relocated page-turn buttons, a real-time clock, and a tilt-to-turn-page feature. They're also lighter and thinner than the X4, though there is a trade-off involved: They drop the USB-C charging port in favor of magnetic pogo pins that require a separate adapter (included).

It has been revealed that these upgrades also increased the cost: The X4 Classic typically retails for $89, $20 more than the discontinued X4 and only $10 less than the X4 Pro, while the X3 debuted at $79. But right now, the X4 Classic is just under $55, or around 38% off, and the X3 is about a dollar more. Either is a great option for those who prioritize crisp, readable text above the conveniences of a built-in light or touchscreen, as those add extra layers between the inner screen and outer glass. It's also important to understand what you're getting into: These devices support only e-books without Digital Rights Management (DRM), which means you can't use it to read your existing library of Kindle books. On the plus side, there's no longer a need to worry about flashing newly introduced firmware if you don't want to, as the native version has been totally overhauled and is now one of your best options (though the new firmware, called "Licorice," isn't available on the X3 quite yet).
